questions.question: How do you design a multi-region architecture — when is active-passive enough vs active-active — and what are the data, latency, and cost trade-offs?
questions.title: Multi-Region Architecture: Active-Passive vs Active-Active, Data Strategies, Trade-offs
questions.direct_answer: Going multi-region is a response to two goals — **disaster recovery** (survive region failure) and/or **low latency** (serve users close to them) — and the right architecture depends on which one drives the decision. **Active-passive** (or pilot light / warm standby) means one region serves, another waits, and data is asynchronously replicated; simpler and cheaper, RPO minutes, RTO minutes-to-hours, no conflict resolution. **Active-active** means multiple regions serve simultaneously; each accepts writes; far more complex but enables low RTO (seconds) and local-latency reads/writes for global users; requires CRDT / last-writer-wins / sharded-by-region data models to avoid conflicts. Middle ground: **read-local / write-home** (reads go local; writes route to home region) works well for user-scoped data. Critical decisions: **data strategy** (synchronous vs async replication, sharding by user/tenant, global vs per-region tables), **traffic routing** (Route 53 geolocation, AWS Global Accelerator, Cloudflare, Kubernetes Federation), **consistency model** (strong vs eventual; by domain), **cross-region networking** (VPC peering, Transit Gateway, private links), and **operational complexity** (deployments, schema migrations, observability across regions, cost). Common traps: underestimating cross-region latency (50–300 ms), assuming 'just replicate the DB' works, ignoring egress costs, and designing for active-active when active-passive with good DR automation would do. Senior move: start active-passive with tested failover, identify which services / data truly need active-active, and evolve incrementally — never convert the whole system at once.

interviewer_intent.system_design: Understanding multi-region trade-offs; data replication strategies; traffic routing; CAP; operational complexity
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Proposing active-active by default; ignoring data consistency challenges; underestimating cost and ops complexity
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss data sharding by region/tenant, CRDT, read-local write-home, egress costs, chaos engineering for failover, incremental migration path

sections.title: Why Multi-Region — and What It Costs You
sections.content:
Most services **do not need multi-region**. A well-run single-region deployment with multi-AZ redundancy handles the overwhelming majority of failure modes. You go multi-region when:

1. **Regulatory / data residency** — user data must stay in specific jurisdictions (GDPR, China, India)
2. **Low latency** — global users can't tolerate 200 ms round-trips to a single region
3. **Region-level disaster recovery** — RTO/RPO requirements the business won't tolerate losing in a region event
4. **Regional scale** — you've outgrown a single region's limits (rare)

Multi-region is **expensive and complicated**:
- 2x+ infrastructure cost
- Cross-region data transfer costs (significant on AWS: ~$0.02/GB)
- Operational overhead: dual deploys, observability correlation, schema migrations
- Data consistency headaches
- Harder debugging (latency + replication lag)

The decision isn't binary. Between 'single region' and 'fully active-active' there's a spectrum: **backup restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-passive, active-active with read-local write-home, full active-active**. Pick the minimum that meets your actual requirements.

sections.title: Multi-Region Patterns Compared
sections.content:
| Pattern | RPO | RTO | Cost (vs single) | Complexity | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Backup + restore** | Hours (last backup) | Hours | 1.1x | Low | Cheap DR; can tolerate long recovery |
| **Pilot light** | Minutes (async replication) | Minutes | 1.3x | Medium | Low RTO without 2x infra |
| **Warm standby** | Seconds-minutes | Seconds-minutes | 1.6x | Medium | Critical prod; still scaling on failover |
| **Active-passive** | Seconds | Seconds-minutes | ~2x | Medium-high | Critical systems with low RTO |
| **Active-active (read-local)** | Seconds | Seconds | 2x+ | High | Global reads with latency SLO |
| **Full active-active** | Sub-second | Sub-second | 2x+ | Very high | Global writes; regulated data residency |

sections.title: Data Strategies — the Hardest Part
sections.content:
**The CAP constraint**: in a network partition, you pick **consistency** or **availability**. Multi-region guarantees partitions will happen — so you explicitly pick where each data domain sits.

**Key patterns:**

**1. Async replication (active-passive, pilot light)**
- Primary accepts writes; replica in remote region follows
- RPO = replication lag (seconds to minutes)
- Failover: promote replica; lose any unreplicated data
- Spring / JDBC: no app change; driver points at primary; on failover, DNS / Route 53 shifts
- Postgres: streaming / logical replication; RDS Multi-AZ + cross-region read replica
- MySQL: async GTID replication; AWS RDS cross-region
- Kafka: MirrorMaker 2.0 / Confluent Replicator

**2. Synchronous replication (strong consistency, pays latency)**
- Every write commits in all regions before ack
- RPO = 0, RTO = seconds if a region dies
- Latency cost: ~50–150 ms per write (intercontinental)
- Use for small, critical, infrequently-written data (config, auth sessions)
- Technologies: Spanner (globally consistent), CockroachDB, Cosmos DB strong tier
- Not viable for high-write workloads across continents

**3. Sharding by region / user / tenant (home region)**
- Each user / tenant has a 'home region'
- Writes for that user go to home region (writes are always local for them)
- Reads can serve from any region (cache / replicate read-only copies)
- Resolution when user moves: rare; migrate their shard
- Works well for B2B SaaS, regional services (banking by country)
- Challenges: cross-user queries; analytics; reports

**4. Multi-master with conflict resolution**
- All regions accept writes; replicate to each other
- Conflicts resolved via:
  - **Last-writer-wins (LWW)** — simplest; can lose data
  - **CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types)** — math guarantees convergence; complex to model
  - **Custom per-field resolution** — e.g., set union for list of items
  - **Application-level reconciliation** — app chooses which wins per field
- Technologies: DynamoDB Global Tables, Cassandra, Cosmos DB multi-region write, Couchbase, Riak, DataDog-style time-series
- Best for high-write workloads that tolerate eventual consistency

**5. Event sourcing + per-region projection**
- Events are the source of truth; each region has read models
- Events replicated across regions (Kafka MirrorMaker, Pulsar GeoReplication)
- Projections rebuilt locally
- Write ordering: total order per stream (partition key)
- Great for analytics, user activity feeds, audit logs

**6. Cache + async writeback**
- Reads served from local cache / replica
- Writes queued locally, propagated to home region async
- User sees their own write via local cache until replication catches up
- Not for critical financial / inventory data

**Data domain classification:**

Not every piece of data needs the same strategy. Classify per domain:

| Domain example | Strategy |
|---|---|
| User profile | Home region per user; cross-region replication |
| Product catalog | Globally replicated, read-only in each region; publish from central |
| Inventory counts | Shard by warehouse; strong consistency within shard |
| Financial transactions | Strong consistency; home region; never multi-master |
| Session tokens | Regional; re-login on failover if necessary |
| Activity feed | Event-sourced; per-region projections |
| Analytics / reports | Replicated via Kafka; central warehouse |
| Auth credentials | Strong consistency (Spanner / Cognito Global) |

This classification is **more important than the technology choice** — it drives everything else.

sections.title: Traffic Routing, Deployment, and Observability
sections.content:
**Traffic routing:**

- **Route 53 geolocation** / **latency-based routing**: DNS directs users to closest region
- **AWS Global Accelerator** / **Cloudflare Argo**: anycast + TCP termination near user; backend across regions
- **CDN (Cloudflare, CloudFront, Fastly)**: for static + edge computing
- **Kubernetes multi-cluster** (Istio, Cilium, Submariner): service mesh across regions
- **API Gateway per region** with global DNS

Failover:
- **Health checks** from DNS / Global Accelerator to regional endpoints
- Automated DNS cutover on unhealthy
- Manual failover for controlled events (avoid flapping)
- Client libraries with regional awareness as fallback (e.g., app reads env-var `REGION` and retries on the other region after N failures)

**Sticky sessions** vs **stateless**:
- If region affinity matters (stateful sessions, local cache), use sticky DNS / cookies
- Stateless services + JWT + distributed cache allow seamless cross-region routing

**Deployment strategies:**

- **Per-region pipelines**: same artifact deployed to each region independently
- **Staged rollout**: region-by-region; catch issues in one region before global impact
- **Canary per region**: 1% traffic in region A to new version; monitor; expand
- **Rollback**: per-region; keep prior image / helm values for fast revert
- **Feature flags** with region scope: enable in one region first

**Schema migrations in multi-region:**
- **Expand-contract** pattern: add new column/table; deploy code handling both; later remove old
- **Bidirectional replication** compatibility: both versions must co-exist
- Never couple schema changes to code deploys in active-active
- Roll out schema changes region by region; let replication catch up before moving to next

**Observability across regions:**
- **Centralized logs** (ELK, Loki, Splunk) with region tags
- **Metrics**: Prometheus federation or managed (Datadog, Grafana Cloud); region as label
- **Tracing**: cross-region trace IDs; headers propagated across regions
- **Dashboards**: global view + per-region; compare latencies, error rates
- **Alerting**: region-aware; per-region SLOs + global SLO

**Testing failover:**
- **Chaos engineering**: inject region failure in staging; verify automated failover works
- **Game days**: quarterly 'lose region X' exercise
- **Backup restore drills**: prove backups actually work; often don't
- **DR runbook**: who pages whom; what buttons to push; rehearsed, not invented during incident

**Cost management:**
- **Cross-region egress**: major cost; design to minimize (only replication traffic, not per-request fan-out)
- **Data transfer in free**, out expensive; design for region-local processing
- **Compute**: 2x regions = 2x compute unless one is scaled-down (pilot light)
- **Storage**: replicated storage doubles cost
- **Optimization**: reserved/savings plans per region; rightsize continuously

**Operational complexity:**
- Teams split ownership by region? or one team owns global?
- Incident response: region-aware runbooks; on-call across time zones
- Compliance: data residency requires data pipeline audits
- Testing: staging multi-region env doubles infra; or use chaos in single staging to simulate

sections.title: Anti-Patterns, Migration, and Senior Engineer Moves
sections.content:
**Anti-patterns:**

1. **Starting with full active-active** when active-passive would do; you've bought complexity without clear benefit
2. **'Just replicate the DB'** — ignores conflict resolution, replication lag, reconciliation
3. **One global DB across regions with synchronous replication** — latency kills write performance
4. **Writing to both regions without home-region routing** — constant conflicts, LWW data loss
5. **Same region names for services + DB** — confusing in ops
6. **Ignoring egress costs** — bills surprise teams
7. **Never testing failover** — DR plan on paper, untested in fire
8. **Schema migrations deployed simultaneously in all regions** — brief downtime; should be staged
9. **One global K8s cluster** — control plane becomes single point of failure
10. **No data residency plan** — GDPR violation when user's data crosses region

**Migration path from single-region to multi-region:**

1. **Assess actual need** — is it DR, latency, residency? Measure current SLOs; talk to product
2. **Make services stateless** — store state in DB / cache; no local disk dependency
3. **Externalize config** — per-region config loaded at startup
4. **Build stateless CI/CD** — same artifact deploys to any region
5. **Set up read replica in new region** — start with active-passive
6. **Practice failover** — game days; automation for DNS / app config
7. **Classify data domains** — per our matrix above
8. **Migrate domains to active-active progressively** — start with read-heavy / cachable
9. **Monitor replication lag, conflict rate** — invest in observability first
10. **Retire single-region patterns** — only once active-active is proven

**Cloud provider specifics:**

*AWS*
- Route 53: geolocation + health checks + failover
- Global Accelerator: anycast + static IPs; faster failover than DNS
- RDS Cross-Region Read Replicas + Aurora Global Database (sub-second replication)
- DynamoDB Global Tables (multi-master)
- S3 Cross-Region Replication
- Kinesis / MSK across regions via MirrorMaker 2.0

*GCP*
- Cloud Load Balancing: global anycast
- Spanner: globally strongly consistent
- Firestore multi-region
- Cloud SQL cross-region read replicas
- Pub/Sub global + regional topics

*Azure*
- Traffic Manager / Front Door: global routing
- Cosmos DB: multi-region, multiple consistency levels
- Azure SQL geo-replication
- Event Hubs Geo-DR

**When multi-region is the wrong answer:**
- DR within a region (multi-AZ) is enough for most
- Single-region at scale serves billions (many services do)
- Multi-cloud ≠ multi-region; solve regional failures first
- Compliance: sometimes multi-region is needed, sometimes it's just one region in a specific country

**Senior engineer moves:**
- **Start with the question**: what problem are we solving? Write it down
- **Quantify the SLOs** — target RPO, RTO, latency budget
- **Run a cost model** — active-active may be 3x single-region when you add egress / data / storage
- **Prototype failover before migration** — don't assume DNS + replica = failover works
- **Classify data domains** — most important design decision
- **Invest in observability first** — you cannot debug multi-region blind
- **Incremental migration** — never flip the switch globally
- **Write runbooks and rehearse** — an untested DR plan is no DR plan
- **Revisit annually** — requirements change; maybe one region is fine now

**Strategic take:**
- Most teams overreach for multi-region; most could solve the underlying problem with better single-region resilience + tested DR
- Multi-region is a **journey**, not a feature flag; start active-passive with automated failover
- Data strategy is the hardest part; get it wrong and everything downstream is harder
- Observability, cost, operational complexity compound — plan for them as much as architecture
- Senior engineers make sure the **business value matches the complexity**

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Go multi-region for DR, latency, or residency** — not by default
- **Active-passive** (simpler, cheaper, async replication) vs **active-active** (complex, expensive, conflict resolution needed)
- Middle ground: **read-local / write-home** often gives 80% of benefits with 30% of complexity
- **Data strategy** is the hardest part: async replication, sync (small data), sharding by region/tenant, multi-master with CRDT/LWW, event sourcing
- **Classify data domains** — not all data gets the same strategy
- **Traffic routing**: Route 53 geolocation, Global Accelerator, Cloudflare, K8s service mesh
- **Failover**: health checks + automated DNS + rehearsed runbooks; chaos test regularly
- **Schema migrations**: expand-contract; staged per region; bidirectional replication compat
- **Observability**: region-tagged logs/metrics/traces; cross-region trace propagation
- **Cost**: 2x+ infra, major egress costs, operational overhead
- **Migrate incrementally** — never flip the switch for the whole system at once
- Revisit the decision yearly; requirements change

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Going multi-region is a response to two goals: disaster recovery (survive region failure) and/or low latency (serve users close to them). The right architecture depends on which drives the decision.

**Active-passive (or pilot light / warm standby)**
- One region serves, another waits
- Data asynchronously replicated
- Simpler and cheaper
- RPO minutes, RTO minutes-to-hours
- No conflict resolution

**Active-active**
- Multiple regions serve simultaneously
- Each accepts writes
- Far more complex but enables low RTO (seconds) and local-latency reads/writes for global users
- Requires CRDT / LWW / sharded-by-region data models to avoid conflicts

**Middle ground: read-local / write-home**
- Reads go local; writes route to home region
- Works well for user-scoped data

**Critical decisions**
- Data strategy (sync vs async replication; shard by user/tenant; global vs per-region tables)
- Traffic routing (Route 53 geolocation, AWS Global Accelerator, Cloudflare, K8s Federation)
- Consistency model (strong vs eventual; by domain)
- Cross-region networking (VPC peering, Transit Gateway, private links)
- Operational complexity (deploys, schema migrations, observability, cost)

**Common traps**
- Underestimating cross-region latency (50-300 ms)
- Assuming 'just replicate the DB' works
- Ignoring egress costs
- Designing active-active when active-passive with good DR automation would do

**Senior move**
- Start active-passive with tested failover
- Identify which services/data truly need active-active
- Evolve incrementally — never convert the whole system at once

**Most services don't need multi-region**
- Well-run single region with multi-AZ handles most failures
- Go multi-region when:
  1. Regulatory/data residency (GDPR, China, India)
  2. Low latency (global users can't tolerate 200 ms to single region)
  3. Region-level DR (RTO/RPO requirements business won't tolerate)
  4. Regional scale (outgrown single region's limits — rare)

**Multi-region is expensive and complicated**
- 2x+ infra cost
- Cross-region data transfer (~$0.02/GB on AWS)
- Operational overhead (dual deploys, observability correlation, schema migrations)
- Data consistency headaches
- Harder debugging (latency + replication lag)

**Spectrum, not binary**
- Backup restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-passive, active-active read-local write-home, full active-active
- Pick minimum meeting actual requirements

**Patterns compared**
| Pattern | RPO | RTO | Cost vs single | Complexity | Use when |
| Backup + restore | Hours | Hours | 1.1x | Low | Cheap DR; tolerate long recovery |
| Pilot light | Minutes | Minutes | 1.3x | Medium | Low RTO without 2x infra |
| Warm standby | Sec-min | Sec-min | 1.6x | Medium | Critical prod; scaling on failover |
| Active-passive | Seconds | Sec-min | ~2x | Medium-high | Critical systems, low RTO |
| Active-active (read-local) | Seconds | Seconds | 2x+ | High | Global reads with latency SLO |
| Full active-active | Sub-sec | Sub-sec | 2x+ | Very high | Global writes; data residency |

**Data strategies — hardest part**

*CAP constraint*
- In a partition, pick consistency or availability
- Multi-region guarantees partitions will happen
- Explicitly pick per data domain

*1. Async replication (active-passive, pilot light)*
- Primary accepts writes; replica follows
- RPO = replication lag (seconds to minutes)
- Failover: promote replica; lose unreplicated data
- Postgres: streaming/logical replication; RDS + cross-region read replica
- MySQL: async GTID; AWS RDS cross-region
- Kafka: MirrorMaker 2.0 / Confluent Replicator

*2. Synchronous replication (strong consistency, pays latency)*
- Every write commits in all regions before ack
- RPO = 0, RTO = seconds
- Cost: ~50-150 ms per write (intercontinental)
- Small, critical, infrequent data (config, auth sessions)
- Technologies: Spanner, CockroachDB, Cosmos DB strong tier
- Not viable for high-write across continents

*3. Sharding by region / user / tenant (home region)*
- Each user/tenant has home region
- Writes for that user go home (always local for them)
- Reads can serve any region (cache / replicate read-only)
- User moves: rare; migrate shard
- Works well B2B SaaS, regional services (banking by country)
- Challenges: cross-user queries, analytics, reports

*4. Multi-master with conflict resolution*
- All regions accept writes; replicate to each other
- Conflicts resolved via:
  - Last-writer-wins (simplest; can lose data)
  - CRDTs (math guarantees convergence; complex to model)
  - Custom per-field (e.g., set union for list of items)
  - Application-level reconciliation
- Technologies: DynamoDB Global Tables, Cassandra, Cosmos DB multi-region write, Couchbase, Riak
- Best for high-write tolerating eventual consistency

*5. Event sourcing + per-region projection*
- Events are source of truth; each region has read models
- Events replicated (Kafka MirrorMaker, Pulsar GeoReplication)
- Projections rebuilt locally
- Write ordering: total order per stream (partition key)
- Great for analytics, activity feeds, audit logs

*6. Cache + async writeback*
- Reads from local cache/replica
- Writes queued locally, propagated to home async
- User sees own write via local cache until replication catches up
- Not for critical financial/inventory

**Data domain classification — more important than technology**
| Domain | Strategy |
| User profile | Home region per user; cross-region replication |
| Product catalog | Globally replicated, read-only; publish from central |
| Inventory counts | Shard by warehouse; strong within shard |
| Financial transactions | Strong consistency; home region; never multi-master |
| Session tokens | Regional; re-login on failover |
| Activity feed | Event-sourced; per-region projections |
| Analytics | Replicated via Kafka; central warehouse |
| Auth credentials | Strong (Spanner / Cognito Global) |

**Traffic routing**
- Route 53 geolocation / latency-based
- AWS Global Accelerator / Cloudflare Argo (anycast + TCP termination near user)
- CDN (Cloudflare, CloudFront, Fastly) for static + edge
- K8s multi-cluster (Istio, Cilium, Submariner)
- API Gateway per region with global DNS

**Failover**
- Health checks from DNS / Global Accelerator to regional endpoints
- Automated DNS cutover on unhealthy
- Manual for controlled events (avoid flapping)
- Client libraries with regional awareness as fallback

**Sticky vs stateless**
- Region affinity matters: sticky DNS/cookies
- Stateless + JWT + distributed cache allows seamless cross-region

**Deployment**
- Per-region pipelines; same artifact independently
- Staged rollout: region-by-region; catch issues before global
- Canary per region: 1% in A, monitor, expand
- Rollback per region; keep prior image/helm values
- Feature flags with region scope

**Schema migrations multi-region**
- Expand-contract: add new column/table; deploy handling both; later remove old
- Bidirectional replication compat: both versions coexist
- Never couple schema to code deploys in active-active
- Roll region by region; let replication catch up

**Observability**
- Centralized logs (ELK, Loki, Splunk) with region tags
- Metrics: Prometheus federation or managed; region as label
- Tracing: cross-region trace IDs; headers propagated
- Dashboards: global + per-region; compare latencies, errors
- Alerting: region-aware; per-region + global SLO

**Testing failover**
- Chaos engineering: inject region failure in staging
- Game days: quarterly 'lose region X'
- Backup restore drills: prove backups actually work
- DR runbook: who pages whom; rehearsed not invented during incident

**Cost management**
- Cross-region egress major cost; design to minimize
- Data in free, out expensive; region-local processing
- Compute: 2x regions = 2x unless scaled-down (pilot light)
- Storage replicated doubles
- Reserved/savings plans per region; rightsize continuously

**Operational complexity**
- Teams split by region or one team owns global?
- Incident response: region-aware runbooks; on-call across time zones
- Compliance: data residency requires audits
- Testing: multi-region staging doubles infra; or chaos in single staging

**Anti-patterns**
1. Starting full active-active when active-passive would do
2. 'Just replicate the DB' — ignores conflicts, lag, reconciliation
3. One global DB with sync replication — latency kills writes
4. Writing to both regions without home-region routing — conflicts, LWW data loss
5. Same region names for services + DB — confusing in ops
6. Ignoring egress costs
7. Never testing failover
8. Schema migrations simultaneously in all regions
9. One global K8s cluster — control plane SPOF
10. No data residency plan — GDPR violation

**Migration path single → multi**
1. Assess actual need (DR, latency, residency?); measure SLOs; talk to product
2. Make services stateless
3. Externalize config (per-region at startup)
4. Stateless CI/CD (same artifact any region)
5. Read replica in new region — start active-passive
6. Practice failover; game days; automation
7. Classify data domains
8. Migrate domains to active-active progressively (start read-heavy/cachable)
9. Monitor replication lag, conflict rate; invest observability first
10. Retire single-region only once active-active proven

**Cloud specifics**

*AWS*
- Route 53 geolocation + health + failover
- Global Accelerator anycast + static IPs; faster failover than DNS
- RDS Cross-Region Read Replicas + Aurora Global Database (sub-second replication)
- DynamoDB Global Tables (multi-master)
- S3 Cross-Region Replication
- Kinesis/MSK across regions via MirrorMaker

*GCP*
- Cloud Load Balancing global anycast
- Spanner globally strongly consistent
- Firestore multi-region
- Cloud SQL cross-region read replicas
- Pub/Sub global + regional topics

*Azure*
- Traffic Manager / Front Door global routing
- Cosmos DB multi-region, multiple consistency
- Azure SQL geo-replication
- Event Hubs Geo-DR

**When multi-region is wrong answer**
- DR within region (multi-AZ) enough for most
- Single region at scale serves billions
- Multi-cloud ≠ multi-region; solve regional failures first
- Compliance sometimes means just one region in specific country

**Senior engineer moves**
- Start with question: what problem solving?
- Quantify SLOs (RPO, RTO, latency budget)
- Cost model — active-active may be 3x when you add egress/data/storage
- Prototype failover before migration
- Classify data domains — most important design decision
- Observability first; can't debug multi-region blind
- Incremental migration; never flip globally
- Runbooks rehearsed; untested DR = no DR
- Revisit annually; requirements change

**Strategic take**
- Most teams overreach for multi-region; could solve underlying problem with better single-region resilience + tested DR
- Multi-region is a journey, not a feature flag
- Start active-passive with automated failover
- Data strategy hardest part; wrong = everything harder
- Observability, cost, ops complexity compound
- Seniors ensure business value matches complexity

**Bottom line**
- Multi-region is advanced engineering; pays off when SLOs require it
- Data model design matters more than any single technology pick
- Start simple, evolve, observe, rehearse failover

beats.text: Anti-patterns: 1. Starting with full active-active when active-passive would do; you've bought complexity without clear benefit 2. 'Just replicate the DB' — ignores conflict resolution, replication lag, reconciliation 3. One global DB across regions with synchronous replication — latency kills write performance 4. Writing to both regions without home-region routing — constant conflicts, LWW data loss 5. Same region names for services + DB — confusing in ops 6. Ignoring egress costs — bills surprise teams 7. Never testing failover — DR plan on paper, untested in fire 8. Schema.

Most services do not need multi-region. A well-run single-region deployment with multi-AZ redundancy handles the overwhelming majority of failure modes. You go multi-region when: 1. Regulatory / data residency — user data must stay in specific jurisdictions (GDPR, China, India) 2. Low latency — global users can't tolerate 200 ms round-trips to a single region 3. Region-level disaster recovery —.
